title: Do I Need a PE Stamp for Shop Drawings in Texas?
metaTitle: PE Stamp for Shop Drawings in Texas: When Needed | PRIMECOST
metaDescription: When do shop drawings need a PE seal in Texas? Learn the difference between detailing and delegated design, what the rules require, and how to avoid rejections.
summary: Shop drawings only need a PE seal in Texas when they contain engineering design. Learn how to tell the difference, what delegated design means, and how to avoid rejected submittals.
content:
The Short Answer

It depends on what the shop drawings contain. In Texas, shop drawings that simply show how a fabricator will build what the engineer of record already designed usually do not need their own engineer's seal. Shop drawings that include new engineering design, such as connection design, delegated components, or elements the fabricator is responsible for designing, generally must be prepared under the responsible charge of a licensed Professional Engineer and sealed.

The deciding question is simple: does the drawing contain engineering decisions that nobody else has already made and sealed? If yes, a PE almost always needs to be involved.

What Shop Drawings Are (and Are Not)

Shop drawings are detailed drawings prepared by a fabricator, supplier, or detailer that show exactly how a component will be made and installed: member sizes, dimensions, bolt patterns, weld symbols, piece marks, and erection sequences. They translate the design documents into something a shop can build.

They are different from the construction documents prepared by the architect and engineer of record. The engineer of record designs the structure. The shop drawings show how that design will be fabricated. The engineer of record then reviews the shop drawings for general conformance with the design intent.

When Shop Drawings Usually Do Not Need a Separate Seal

  • Steel detailing where all members, connections, and loads are fully designed and shown on the engineer of record's sealed drawings.
  • Rebar placing drawings that follow the sizes, spacing, and laps already specified in the structural drawings.
  • Architectural or millwork shop drawings with no structural or life-safety design content.

In these cases the detailer is drafting, not designing. The engineering responsibility stays with the engineer of record, whose seal is already on the design documents.

When Shop Drawings Usually Do Need a PE Seal

  • Delegated connection design: the structural drawings give loads and ask the fabricator to design the steel connections. Those connection designs and calculations are engineering and need a PE.
  • Delegated design components: items such as pre-engineered metal buildings, wood or cold-formed steel trusses, precast concrete, curtain walls, metal stairs and railings, and some shoring or temporary works are often designed by the supplier's engineer and submitted with sealed drawings and calculations.
  • Substitutions or changes: if the fabricator proposes a different member, connection, or system than what was designed, the change needs engineering review and usually a seal.
  • Deferred submittals required by the building official: when the permit lists deferred submittals, the building department typically expects sealed drawings and calculations for those items.

How Texas Law Frames It

Engineering in Texas is regulated by the Texas Board of Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors under the Texas Engineering Practice Act. In general terms, engineering work must be performed by, or under the responsible charge of, a Texas-licensed PE, and engineering documents released for construction must be sealed by that engineer. Firms that offer engineering services in Texas must also be registered with the Board.

That is why the question is really about content, not the name of the drawing. Calling something a "shop drawing" does not exempt it from sealing if it contains engineering design. Always check the project specifications and ask the engineer of record which submittals must be sealed.

Read the Specifications First

Most projects spell this out. Look for sections titled "delegated design," "submittals," or "deferred submittals" in the specifications, and check the general notes on the structural drawings. They usually list which components the contractor must have designed by a licensed engineer, what calculations are required, and who must seal them.

Common Mistakes That Get Submittals Rejected

  • Submitting delegated connection or truss designs without calculations.
  • Sealing by an engineer who is not licensed in Texas.
  • Changing members or connections on shop drawings without flagging the change to the engineer of record.
  • Missing the deferred submittal list on the permit, which delays inspections.

faq.question: Do steel shop drawings need a PE stamp in Texas?
faq.answer: Not when they only detail members and connections already designed and sealed by the engineer of record. If the fabricator designs connections or other elements, that engineering must be done by a Texas-licensed PE and sealed.

faq.question: What is delegated design?
faq.answer: Delegated design is when the construction documents assign the design of a specific component, such as connections, trusses, or curtain walls, to the contractor or supplier, who must have it designed and sealed by a licensed engineer.

faq.question: Can an out-of-state engineer seal Texas shop drawings?
faq.answer: Engineering documents for Texas projects generally must be sealed by an engineer licensed in Texas, working for a firm registered with the Texas Board of Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors.

faq.question: How do I know which submittals need a seal?
faq.answer: Check the specifications for delegated design and deferred submittal sections, read the general notes on the structural drawings, and confirm with the engineer of record.
